title: How to Get Smoke Smell Out of Clothes

excerpt: Smoke odor clings to fibers and oily residues, so airing helps but may not be enough. The right cleaning approach depends on whether the exposure was light ambient smoke or a fire involving soot and other contaminants.
content_html:
Smoke odor clings to fibers and oily residues, so airing helps but may not be enough. The right cleaning approach depends on whether the exposure was light ambient smoke or a fire involving soot and other contaminants.

Air garments out before washing after light exposure

Hang clothes in a well-ventilated area, protected from strong sun if the fabric is sensitive. This can reduce volatile odor compounds before you put heavily scented garments into the washer.

Use the correct detergent dose

Separate heavily affected items and wash at the warmest temperature allowed by the care label. Excess detergent can leave residue that holds odor; an extra rinse can help when product remains in the fabric.

Do not mix cleaners to chase the odor

Do not combine bleach, vinegar, ammonia, or other additives. If you use an odor-removal product or oxygen bleach, follow its label and make sure it is compatible with the color and fiber.

Fire soot needs greater caution

Clothes coated in soot, chemical residue, or fire-suppression water may require professional cleaning or disposal. Shaking soot indoors redistributes particles, so follow fire-restoration and safety guidance rather than treating it like ordinary smoke odor.
